node.description: A verbatim transcript of the words spoken or sung in the video.

The primary language spoken or sung in the video — if several are used, give the one used most. Provide an English name (e.g. 'English', 'Mandarin', 'Arabic'). Use '-' if there is no spoken or sung language (music-only or silent).
Are multiple languages spoken or sung in the video (e.g. code-switching, or different speakers using different languages)? Answer No if there is no speech or only one language is used.
Notable objects visible in the video.
Visible symbols, flags, or brands.
On-screen text, transcribed via OCR.
Each distinct face that appears in the video, with its gender, apparent age range (e.g. 20-30), and apparent ethnicity.

speech_vs_music.description: the percentage of the audio that is spoken word (0 = all music/other, 100 = all speech)

background_music.description: the style or mood of any background music

node.description: The video's audio profile: how much of the audio is speech (as a percentage of speech vs music/other), the style/mood of any background music, and any notable sounds or sound effects.
The main activity, as a verb + object, e.g. 'dancing in a studio'.
A concise narrative summary of the entire video.
The narrative type of the video.

The TikTok content categories that best capture the video's dominant focus (up to two; list the most central first). Weigh whether the video's primary purpose is entertainment & cultural expression, lifestyle & personal content, or informative & advisory content, then choose the most fitting category.

The country the video is primarily connected to — through the creator's origin (accent, language, location tags, or profile), the content's subject matter (events, places, landmarks, or social issues), or its intended audience (region-specific hashtags or localised references). Give the single most-connected country as an English name (e.g. 'Australia', 'United States', 'India'). Use '-' when there is no clear country connection (generic or globally-oriented content).

Is the video produced primarily for TikTok — vertical/portrait, short (typically under 60 seconds), using TikTok's native features (filters, effects, text overlays, trending sounds) and pacing? Answer No for content clearly made for another platform (e.g. a longer YouTube or TV-style video) and merely reposted to TikTok.

Does the video leverage a technical TikTok trend — a trending template, effect, or sound used to make it (e.g. a CapCut 'try this effect' or 'use this sound' template)? A video can be both a technical and a cultural trend.

Does the video replicate a cultural TikTok trend — a participatory format meant for other creators to imitate (e.g. a dance challenge, meme, or format like 'candy salad')? A video can be both a technical and a cultural trend.

Is the video an explicit paid promotion of a product, service, or brand — shown by a sponsorship label, repeated prominent brand mentions, or a direct call to purchase or visit? Answer No for an organic review or discussion, or a creator simply expressing affinity for a brand with no sign of a commercial agreement.

Is the video primarily AI-generated — AI-generated elements forming a substantial part of it (e.g. prompt-generated footage), or explicitly labelled AI-generated by the creator or platform? Answer No when only minor AI elements are present (e.g. AI stickers, memes, or background music).
The gender of the main person featured in the video.
The ethnicity of the main person featured in the video.
How political the video is, from 0 (not at all) to 100 (entirely political).
How sensitive the video's subject matter is, from 0 (not at all) to 100 (extremely sensitive).
The action the video encourages the viewer to take, or '-' if none.
